title: Exploiting chemical shift variability enables recovery of overlapping metabolites from 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectra
summary: Overlapping peaks and sample-dependent chemical shift variability prevent reliable metabolite recovery from complex biological spectra. This problem is critical in one-dimensional proton (1D 1H) NMR which has become the standard method providing fast acquisition and information-rich spectra in metabolomics and foodomics. This study demonstrates how chemical shifts can be utilised as a strength in 1D 1H NMR, when suitably modeled through the proposed Bayesian Shift-Invariant Non-negative Matrix Factorization (BSI-NMF) procedure. We find that BSI-NMF accurately recovers the underlying chemical signals in 1D 1H NMR spectra missed by existing analyses approaches across simulations, laboratory created datasets, and a large urine dataset obtained from 2439 people across Europe. Our study highlights how shifts in the chemical signatures - until now perceived as a nuisance - can in fact when suitably modelled be instrumental for unique recovery of metabolites. This creates an opportunity to experimentally induce chemical shifts changes to facilitate unique recovery of spectra.

AI.tldr: BSI-NMF is a Bayesian Shift-Invariant Non-negative Matrix Factorization method that models chemical shifts in 1D 1H NMR spectra to accurately recover overlapping metabolite signals, validated across simulations, lab datasets, and a 2439-person European urine dataset, outperforming existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Overlapping peaks and sample-dependent chemical shift variability prevent reliable metabolite recovery from complex biological spectra, particularly in 1D 1H NMR—the standard method for metabolomics and foodomics. Chemical shifts have traditionally been viewed as a nuisance rather than a useful signal feature.
AI.method: The authors propose Bayesian Shift-Invariant Non-negative Matrix Factorization (BSI-NMF), which explicitly models chemical shifts as part of the factorization procedure, turning shift variability from a problem into an informative feature for metabolite recovery.
AI.result: BSI-NMF accurately recovers underlying chemical signals in 1D 1H NMR spectra that existing analysis approaches miss, demonstrated across simulations, laboratory-created datasets, and a large urine dataset from 2439 individuals across Europe.
AI.conclusion: Chemical shifts, previously perceived as a nuisance, can be instrumental for unique metabolite recovery when suitably modeled, opening opportunities to experimentally induce chemical shift changes to facilitate unique spectral recovery.

title: JUMP-lite: Compact, reproducible benchmarking of cell representations
summary: Image-based profiling captures rich phenotypic signatures for drug discovery and functional genomics. Large public datasets like JUMP Cell Painting now provide millions of images for systematic study. However, the scale of these resources, 115 TB for JUMP alone, and fragmented evaluation practices make systematic comparison of representation methods intractable for many researchers. Here we present Nahual, an open-source framework for reproducible model deployment, and JUMP-lite, a curated 116 GB subset of JUMP that is 1000 times smaller while preserving phenotypic diversity through careful selection of perturbations with high-confidence annotations and a storage reduction via lossy JPEG XL compression. With these, we benchmark five representation methods, including classical features (CellProfiler) and deep learning models (MorphEM, OpenPhenom, SubCell, DINOv2), and demonstrate that compression preserves downstream signal while standardized phenotypic activity and consistency metrics reveal meaningful performance differences across methods. Together, JUMP-lite and Nahual provide a foundation for accessible, reproducible benchmarking of image-based cell representations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Nahual, an open-source framework for reproducible model deployment, and JUMP-lite, a curated 116 GB subset of the 115 TB JUMP Cell Painting dataset that is 1000x smaller while preserving phenotypic diversity via careful perturbation selection and lossy JPEG XL compression. The authors benchmark five representation methods (CellProfiler, MorphEM, OpenPhenom, SubCell, DINOv2) and demonstrate that compression preserves downstream signal while standardized metrics reveal meaningful performance differences.
AI.motivation: Image-based profiling produces rich phenotypic signatures for drug discovery and functional genomics, but large public datasets like JUMP (115 TB) are too large for many researchers, and fragmented evaluation practices prevent systematic comparison of representation methods.
AI.method: The authors create JUMP-lite, a curated 116 GB subset of JUMP that is 1000x smaller, preserving phenotypic diversity through careful selection of perturbations with high-confidence annotations and storage reduction via lossy JPEG XL compression. They also develop Nahual, an open-source framework for reproducible model deployment, and benchmark five representation methods including classical features (CellProfiler) and deep learning models (MorphEM, OpenPhenom, SubCell, DINOv2) using standardized phenotypic activity and consistency metrics.
AI.result: Benchmarking results demonstrate that JPEG XL compression preserves downstream signal while standardized phenotypic activity and consistency metrics reveal meaningful performance differences across the five representation methods tested.
AI.conclusion: JUMP-lite and Nahual provide a foundation for accessible, reproducible benchmarking of image-based cell representations, making large-scale phenotypic profiling more tractable for the broader research community.

title: Permutation theory governs long-term dynamics of critical Boolean networks
summary: Boolean networks are widely used to model gene regulatory dynamics, where long-term behavior is organized by attractors - by both their number and their lengths. The number of attractors was resolved recently, but the distribution of attractor lengths and its dependence on network architecture remain poorly understood. We address this for critical Boolean networks with connectivity $K=1$. We show that the attractor structure of these networks is encoded by a permutation induced by the network's feedback loops, thereby recasting questions about attractor lengths as questions about permutations and their arithmetic properties. In particular, the maximum attractor length is determined by the order of the induced permutation. Using results of Erdős and Turán together with a classical theorem of Landau, we show that almost all networks have attractors of length at most $\exp[\tfrac{1}{2}\ln^2 N]$, while some networks support attractors as long as $\exp[\sqrt{N\ln N}]$. The mean attractor length scales as $\exp[N^{1/3}]$, reflecting the influence of rare networks whose exceptionally long attractors dominate the expectation value. These results establish a direct connection between Boolean network dynamics, combinatorics, and number theory, and identify the permutation induced by the feedback loops as a central dynamical invariant governing attractor lengths in critical Boolean networks.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes attractor lengths in critical Boolean networks with connectivity K=1, showing that the attractor structure is encoded by a permutation induced by the network's feedback loops. Using results from Erdős–Turán and Landau's theorem, they prove that almost all networks have attractors of length at most exp[½ ln² N], while rare networks can support attractors as long as exp[√(N ln N)], with the mean attractor length scaling as exp[N^{1/3}] due to the dominance of rare networks with exceptionally long attractors.
AI.motivation: While the number of attractors in Boolean networks has been recently resolved, the distribution of attractor lengths and its dependence on network architecture (topology) remains poorly understood. This paper aims to fill this gap for the specific case of critical Boolean networks with connectivity K=1.
AI.method: The authors show that the attractor structure of critical Boolean networks with K=1 is encoded by a permutation induced by the network's feedback loops. This recasts questions about attractor lengths as questions about permutations and their arithmetic properties. They then apply results from Erdős and Turán (on permutation statistics) together with Landau's theorem (on the maximal order of elements in the symmetric group) to derive bounds on attractor lengths.
AI.result: Almost all networks have attractors of length at most exp[½ ln² N], while some networks support attractors as long as exp[√(N ln N)]. The mean attractor length scales as exp[N^{1/3}], reflecting the influence of rare networks whose exceptionally long attractors dominate the expectation value.
AI.conclusion: The authors establish a direct connection between Boolean network dynamics, combinatorics, and number theory. The permutation induced by feedback loops is identified as a central dynamical invariant governing attractor lengths in critical Boolean networks.

title: MAPK Pathway Activity and Heme Biosynthesis Gene Expression in IDH-Wildtype Glioblastoma: A Purity-Adjusted, Discovery-Validation Analysis
summary: 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) promotes fluorescence-based resection of glioblastoma via protoporphyrin IX (PpIX); however, there is considerable heterogeneity in fluorescence intensity, limiting margin distinction. Cell-line studies show that stimulation of the MAPK pathway results in decreased PpIX levels through increased elimination by ABCB1, an efflux transporter, and ferrochelatase (FECH), the enzyme that converts PpIX to heme. However, the mechanism has yet to be studied in human tissue. Using two independent, purity-adjusted sets of primary IDH-wildtype glioblastoma specimens (TCGA-GBM, n=140, discovery; CGGA, n=87, validation), no reproducible correlation between MAPK signaling and its proposed downstream effectors (ABCB1 and FECH) could be detected. Instead, MAPK activity displayed a reproducibly negative relationship with PPOX, the enzyme that converts protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX: TCGA-GBM (n=133 with purity estimates; rho = -0.40, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.54, -0.25], adjusted p < 0.001), CGGA (rho = -0.28, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.47, -0.07], adjusted p = 0.0342). The finding was robust to permutation testing and to alternative approaches to purity adjustment. Here we report, for the first time, replicated human-tissue evidence for this association. If this correlation reflects causality, MAPK regulation of PpIX would act at the point of synthesis rather than at the clearance steps implied by previous cell-culture studies. We observed differential activation of the MAPK pathway with increased activation in the classical subtype and decreased activation in the proneural subtype. There was no correlation between MAPK pathway activation and overall survival (log-rank p = 0.73). The association between PPOX expression and MAPK pathway activation is biological rather than prognostic, identifying the MAPK pathway as a candidate handle for increasing 5-ALA fluorescence.

AI.tldr: This study provides the first replicated human-tissue evidence that MAPK pathway activation is negatively associated with PPOX (the enzyme synthesizing protoporphyrin IX) in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, suggesting MAPK regulates PpIX at the synthesis step rather than the clearance step implied by prior cell-line work. Differential MAPK activation was seen across molecular subtypes, but no prognostic correlation was found.
AI.motivation: 5-ALA-based fluorescence resection of glioblastoma relies on PpIX accumulation, but fluorescence intensity is highly heterogeneous, limiting tumor margin distinction. Prior cell-line studies suggested MAPK pathway stimulation reduces PpIX via increased ABCB1 efflux and FECH clearance, yet this mechanism had never been validated in human tissue.
AI.method: Two independent purity-adjusted cohorts of primary IDH-wildtype glioblastoma were analyzed (TCGA-GBM discovery, n=140; CGGA validation, n=87). Spearman correlations between MAPK activity and proposed downstream effectors (ABCB1, FECH, PPOX) were assessed with bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation testing, and alternative purity-adjustment approaches.
AI.result: No reproducible correlation was found between MAPK signaling and ABCB1/FECH. Instead, MAPK activity showed a reproducible negative correlation with PPOX in both cohorts (TCGA: rho=-0.40, p<0.001; CGGA: rho=-0.28, p=0.034), robust to permutation and purity-adjustment methods. MAPK activation was higher in classical and lower in proneural subtypes, with no correlation to overall survival (log-rank p=0.73).
AI.conclusion: MAPK regulation of PpIX in human glioblastoma likely acts at the synthesis step via PPOX rather than the clearance steps implied by cell culture. This association is biological, not prognostic, positioning the MAPK pathway as a candidate therapeutic handle to enhance 5-ALA fluorescence for improved surgical resection.

title: Sensorimotor features of a reversal learning task bias decision behavior without disrupting individual difference structure
summary: In computational psychiatry, task-irrelevant factors such as a task's perceptual and motor features are typically assumed not to bias decision behavior, but at most to add noise. Yet growing evidence links sensorimotor processing to decision-making through multiple pathways, challenging this assumption. We tested this directly using a two-choice probabilistic reversal learning task completed by 90 participants under two sensorimotor conditions: a stationary condition requiring only arm movements to respond, and an active condition requiring participants to walk between physically separated computers. Task performance, measured as the propensity to choose the more probable rewarding option, did not differ between conditions. However, stay rate (the tendency to repeat the previous choice) was significantly elevated in the stationary condition, but only among participants who completed the active condition first; those who completed the stationary condition first showed no such difference. Logistic regression weights capturing the influence of recent win history on choice showed the same pattern, with stationary-condition elevation restricted to the active-first group. Cross-condition correlations for both measures were strong, indicating that this order-dependent effect shifted absolute measurements without disrupting individual difference structure. Prior sensorimotor history therefore does not compromise the task's ability to extract stable cognitive variables, but does bias the values it yields - a non-random source of variance that, if it generalizes beyond this experiment, could shift patients across diagnostic thresholds in proposed clinical applications. The finding adds to a growing list of potential methodological contaminants in computational psychiatry's cognitive-task paradigms that must be characterized and mitigated before clinical translation.

AI.tldr: This study tested whether task-irrelevant sensorimotor demands bias decision-making in a probabilistic reversal learning task. While task performance didn't differ between stationary and active (walking) conditions, stay rate and win-history influence were significantly elevated in the stationary condition—but only for participants who completed the active condition first. This order-dependent effect shifted absolute measurements without disrupting individual difference structure, suggesting sensorimotor history biases cognitive measurement values but not their stability.
AI.motivation: Computational psychiatry assumes task-irrelevant sensorimotor factors only add noise to decision behavior, yet growing evidence links sensorimotor processing to decision-making through multiple pathways. This assumption needs direct testing because if sensorimotor factors bias decision variables, they could shift patients across diagnostic thresholds in clinical applications.
AI.method: 90 participants completed a two-choice probabilistic reversal learning task under two sensorimotor conditions: a stationary condition (arm movements only) and an active condition (walking between physically separated computers). Task performance (propensity to choose the more probable rewarding option), stay rate (tendency to repeat previous choice), and logistic regression weights for recent win history were compared across conditions and order of completion.
AI.result: Task performance did not differ between conditions. Stay rate was significantly elevated in the stationary condition, but only for participants who completed the active condition first; no such difference was seen for those completing the stationary condition first. Logistic regression weights for win history showed the same order-dependent pattern. Cross-condition correlations were strong for both measures, indicating the effect shifted absolute measurements without disrupting individual difference structure.
AI.conclusion: Prior sensorimotor history biases the absolute values of cognitive measurements without compromising their stability across individuals. This represents a non-random source of variance that, if generalizable, could shift patients across diagnostic thresholds in clinical applications. The finding adds to the list of methodological contaminants in computational psychiatry that must be characterized and mitigated before clinical translation.

title: Approximate Analytical Protein Distributions for the Three-stage Model of Stochastic Gene Expression
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; submitted to Physical Review E
summary: Gene expression is an intrinsically stochastic process that generates phenotypic heterogeneity within genetically identical cell populations. While the exact statistical moments of the protein count can be obtained for a broad range of complex models, the corresponding distributions are significantly harder to obtain and intractable in many cases. The classical three-stage model of gene expression, which predicts fluctuations in protein levels as a function of promoter switching, transcription, translation, and degradation events all occurring with linear propensities, illustrates this perfectly; deriving its exact protein distribution remains elusive. Here, using the partitioning property of time-inhomogeneous Poisson processes, we develop an exact mapping of the three-stage model onto a simplified model. The simplified model allows us to formulate two analytical approximations for the full protein distribution of the three-stage model based on a beta-mixture representation of the exact solution for a simpler model. We show that the two approximations are asymptotically exact in different limiting cases and verify their accuracy against simulations for a broad range of parameters. Although approximate, these are the first analytical expressions for protein distributions for the three-stage model that are highly accurate in intermediate regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper develops the first accurate analytical approximations for the protein count distribution of the classical three-stage model of gene expression, using a beta-mixture representation derived from an exact mapping via the partitioning property of time-inhomogeneous Poisson processes.
AI.motivation: While exact statistical moments of protein counts can be computed for complex gene expression models, the full protein distributions remain intractable for many cases, including the classical three-stage model. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing analytical expressions for the protein distribution in this widely used model.
AI.method: The authors exploit the partitioning property of time-inhomogeneous Poisson processes to establish an exact mapping of the three-stage model onto a simplified model. This simplification enables the formulation of two analytical approximations for the full protein distribution, based on a beta-mixture representation of the exact solution for the simpler model.
AI.result: The two approximations are shown to be asymptotically exact in different limiting cases and verified against simulations across a broad range of parameters. They are highly accurate in intermediate regimes, marking the first analytical expressions for protein distributions of the three-stage model that perform well in these scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides practical, accurate analytical approximations for protein distributions in the three-stage gene expression model, addressing a longstanding gap where exact distributions were elusive.

title: Mutual-Information-Dependent Nonlinear Threshold Response Model Linked to the Free Energy Principle
summary: Biological systems not only infer states of the external world from sensory input but also vary the expression of their responses according to the information they have acquired. Here, without altering the standard inferential and policy-evaluation schemes of the Free Energy Principle (FEP) and active inference, we propose a minimal dynamics that links the mutual information formed between an external state and an internal representation through inference to a response-expression variable distinct from policy selection. In this formulation, established information is positioned as a state signal that modulates response expression. The model introduces a piecewise nonlinear term in which response activation is driven only when mutual information exceeds an information threshold. Monte Carlo simulations using a two-state Markov environment showed that increasing observation accuracy increased the mutual information between the external state and the internal representation and, in turn, increased response activation. By contrast, in a control condition without information-response coupling, the response remained at its baseline level. The basic pattern of response activation was preserved when observation accuracy, the information-response coupling coefficient, the information threshold, and the closed-loop coefficient linking response to sensory sampling were varied. These results show that coupling information formed by FEP-consistent inference to an independent response-expression dynamics can generate a nonlinear response that depends on an information threshold.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a minimal dynamics that links mutual information (formed through FEP-consistent inference between external states and internal representations) to a response-expression variable, using a piecewise nonlinear term where response activation occurs only when mutual information exceeds a threshold. Monte Carlo simulations in a two-state Markov environment confirm that higher observation accuracy increases mutual information and thereby response activation, and the pattern is robust across parameter variations.
AI.motivation: Biological systems vary their response expression based on acquired information, but standard Free Energy Principle (FEP) and active inference frameworks do not explicitly link information gain to response expression distinct from policy selection. The authors aim to bridge this gap without altering standard inferential and policy-evaluation schemes.
AI.method: The authors introduce a piecewise nonlinear term where response activation is driven only when mutual information exceeds an information threshold. The approach preserves standard FEP inference and policy evaluation, adds a response-expression variable, and couples it to the mutual information between external states and internal representations. Simulations use a two-state Markov environment with a control condition lacking information-response coupling.
AI.result: Monte Carlo simulations showed that increasing observation accuracy increased mutual information and response activation. In the control condition without coupling, responses remained at baseline. The response activation pattern was robust across variations in observation accuracy, coupling coefficient, information threshold, and closed-loop coefficient.
AI.conclusion: Coupling information formed by FEP-consistent inference to an independent response-expression dynamics can generate a nonlinear, threshold-dependent response, offering a minimal mechanism within the FEP/active inference framework for how acquired information modulates response expression.

title: Ancient DNA in motion: Studying past human mobility and interactions by integrating archaeogenetics and archaeology
summary: Here, we present an overview of how archaeogenomic data can be used to investigate past mobilities and how it can be integrated with archaeological research to reconstruct models of human mobility at different scales. We first seek to explain the importance of a clear terminological and theoretical approach to mobility, discussing terms such as migration, admixture, ancestry, and replacement. We then describe the theoretical principles and state-of-the-art tools for inferring past mobility from ancient DNA data, including exploratory approaches and formal modeling, and the relevance of using diverse lines of evidence including allele-frequency patterns, haplotype-sharing, genetic relatedness, and uniparental markers. We further discuss the power and limitations of these methods for inferring different modes of mobility, such as large-scale and long-distance mobility, which we refer to as migration, and also small-scale and short-distance movements, which we argue constituted the bulk of past human mobility and may have had the major share in shaping cultural landscapes. We also describe inference of sex-biased mobility events. Finally, we present examples of joint analyses of genomic data with archaeological, bioarchaeological and historical evidence, demonstrating the potential of interdisciplinary analyses in building comprehensive models of past mobilities. We finish by calling for further integration across fields.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an overview of how ancient DNA (archaeogenomic) data can be used to investigate past human mobility, discussing terminological frameworks, analytical tools, and interdisciplinary integration with archaeological evidence across different spatial and temporal scales.
AI.motivation: To clarify terminology and theoretical approaches to mobility research, and to demonstrate how ancient DNA can be integrated with archaeological evidence to build comprehensive models of past human movement at different scales.
AI.method: The paper reviews theoretical principles and state-of-the-art computational tools for inferring mobility from ancient DNA, including exploratory approaches and formal modeling, using diverse evidence types (allele-frequency patterns, haplotype-sharing, genetic relatedness, uniparental markers), and presents case studies of interdisciplinary (genomic+archaeological+bioarchaeological+historical) analyses.
AI.result: The paper delineates distinctions between large-scale migration and small-scale short-distance mobility (argued to be the bulk of past human movement), discusses sex-biased mobility inference, and demonstrates the power and limitations of various analytical methods through joint interdisciplinary analyses.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for further integration across genetics, archaeology, bioarchaeology, and history to build comprehensive models of past human mobility.

title: Graph Analysis of Neuronal-Culture Connectivity Derived from a Reservoir-Computing Model
summary: Graph-theoretical analysis offers a principled framework for quantifying emergent dynamics in neuronal cultures. Here, we present an analytical pipeline for inferring network-level properties of in vitro cortical cultures from multichannel electrophysiological recordings. The approach builds on a recently proposed Reservoir Computing (RC) framework (Auslender et al., 2025), which enables direct extraction of an Intrinsic Connectivity Map (ICM) from neural activity. We interpret the ICM as an effective adjacency matrix and apply graph-theoretic centrality measures to quantify node- and edge-level contributions to the culture's collective dynamics. We systematically evaluate both local and global graph metrics and examine their relationships with experimentally measured activity features, including firing rates and network-level descriptors. To validate the inference procedure, we also simulate the experimental environment, enabling controlled benchmarking of the RC-derived connectivity against a known ground-truth adjacency matrix and assessment of model performance as a function of graph structure. Our results demonstrate statistically robust associations, of varying strength, between graph-theoretic measures and experimentally observed activity patterns. These findings additionally support the validity of the RC-based connectivity inference and establish a scalable, data-driven framework for functional network characterization in neuronal culture systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an analytical pipeline that applies graph-theoretic centrality measures to an Intrinsic Connectivity Map (ICM) derived from a Reservoir Computing framework, to quantify network-level properties of in vitro cortical cultures from multichannel electrophysiological recordings. The approach is validated through simulations with known ground-truth connectivity and demonstrates statistically robust associations between graph metrics and experimentally observed activity patterns.
AI.motivation: There is a need for principled, data-driven frameworks to quantify emergent dynamics and network-level properties in neuronal cultures. Graph-theoretical analysis offers such a framework, but requires reliable connectivity inference from multichannel electrophysiological recordings, which remains a key challenge.
AI.method: The approach builds on a Reservoir Computing (RC) framework (Auslender et al., 2025) to extract an Intrinsic Connectivity Map (ICM) from neural activity, interpreted as an effective adjacency matrix. Graph-theoretic centrality measures are applied to quantify node- and edge-level contributions. Both local and global graph metrics are systematically evaluated and compared against experimentally measured activity features. Validation is performed through simulations of the experimental environment, enabling benchmarking against known ground-truth adjacency matrices and assessment of model performance as a function of graph structure.
AI.result: The results demonstrate statistically robust associations, of varying strength, between graph-theoretic measures and experimentally observed activity patterns. The findings support the validity of the RC-based connectivity inference approach.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a scalable, data-driven framework for functional network characterization in neuronal culture systems, validating the Reservoir Computing-based connectivity inference and demonstrating the utility of graph-theoretic analysis in neuronal culture research.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Missing-Data Multimodal Latent for Fetal-Growth Analysis
summary: Objective: Routine third-trimester examination yields fetal biometry, maternal, Doppler and fetal-cardiac measurements, acquired at clinical discretion and therefore often incomplete. We show that these four measurement blocks are close to mutually uninformative, and that this single property determines what a representation of them can impute, what it can audit, and what fetal size alone cannot indicate. Methods: A linear-Gaussian factor model (K = 8 by parallel analysis, VARIMAX-rotated) was fitted to 25 measurements in four blocks from 977 fetuses (169 SGA, 61 severe; 77 LGA). Posterior precision sums contributions from observed measurements only, so missing values are marginalized rather than imputed. Data quality was screened using the standardized residual between each measurement and its reconstruction. Results: Predicting any one block from the other three gives an out-of-fold R2 of 0.023. The representation is a continuous growth spectrum with no cluster structure (Hartigan dip p = 0.99, gap statistic k = 1, three-cluster silhouette 0.07) ordering fetuses by birthweight centile (Spearman rho = 0.55). Among 169 SGA fetuses the haemodynamic redistribution axis separated the 25 adverse outcomes (AUC 0.70, 0.585-0.808) where measured size did not (0.60, 0.451-0.738). With Doppler censored, the marginalized interval covered held-out measurements in 97% and 93% of cases against nominal 95% and 90%. The reconstruction residual flagged 38 of 977 records, 36 confirmed transcription errors in the registry. Conclusion: Marginalizing missing measurements yields a representation whose uncertainty reflects the available data, and whose reconstruction residual doubles as a data-quality screen. Because the blocks are nearly independent, confirmed flags are within-block errors, and a synthetic benchmark gives the coupling needed before cross-block detection becomes available.

AI.tldr: A linear-Gaussian factor model fitted to 25 third-trimester fetal measurements across four blocks (biometry, maternal, Doppler, fetal-cardiac) reveals that these blocks are nearly mutually uninformative. Missing values are marginalized rather than imputed, yielding a continuous growth spectrum that orders fetuses by birthweight centile, provides a haemodynamic redistribution axis that predicts adverse SGA outcomes better than size alone, and produces reconstruction residuals that serve as an effective data-quality screen (flagging 36 confirmed transcription errors).
AI.motivation: Routine third-trimester fetal examination produces incomplete measurements because acquisition is at clinical discretion, and the structure of what can be imputed, audited, or inferred from the available data was poorly understood.
AI.method: A linear-Gaussian factor model (K=8, VARIMAX-rotated) was fitted to 25 measurements across four blocks from 977 fetuses (169 SGA, 61 severe; 77 LGA). Missing values are marginalized (posterior precision sums contributions from observed measurements only). Data quality was screened via standardized residuals between each measurement and its reconstruction; block predictability was assessed via out-of-fold R2.
AI.result: Predicting any one block from the other three gives out-of-fold R2 of 0.023. The representation is a continuous growth spectrum (no cluster structure) ordering fetuses by birthweight centile (rho=0.55). The haemodynamic redistribution axis separated 25 adverse SGA outcomes (AUC 0.70) where measured size did not (0.60). Marginalized intervals covered held-out measurements at 97%/93% vs nominal 95%/90%. Reconstruction residuals flagged 38 records, 36 confirmed transcription errors.
AI.conclusion: Marginalizing missing measurements yields a representation whose uncertainty reflects available data, and whose reconstruction residual serves as a data-quality screen. Because blocks are nearly independent, confirmed flags are within-block errors; synthetic benchmarks provide the coupling needed before cross-block detection becomes possible.

title: Hit Selection Using SSMD-Based Machine Learning Performance Metrics in High-Throughput Screening Assays
summary: High-throughput screening (HTS) assays are central to early-stage drug discovery but are often limited by extreme data sparsity, as primary screens typically use only a single replicate per test substance. This sparsity makes conventional machine-learning performance metrics, such as sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), difficult to estimate empirically because they require adequately sized labeled samples. Here, we introduce a model-based framework that derives these classification metrics from the strictly standardized mean difference (SSMD), a well-established HTS effect-size parameter. Under a Gaussian equal-variance assumption, we derive closed-form relationships linking SSMD to Youden-optimal sensitivity and specificity, and sensitivity at a preset specificity, yielding explicit estimators and exact confidence intervals from the noncentral t-distribution, even under single-replicate designs. Unlike classical statistical power, which approaches 1 as sample size grows regardless of how small the true non-zero difference between group means is, the SSMD-derived sensitivity converges to a finite population value that reflects the true degree of separation between two groups, making it a more meaningful and stable performance measure for hit selection. We demonstrate the utility of this framework in a hepatitis C virus primary siRNA screen comprising approximately 22,000 single-replicate measurements, showing that SSMD, AUROC, and sensitivity-based thresholds yield equivalent and interpretable hit sets. This work bridges classical HTS statistics and machine-learning evaluation theory, providing a statistically principled, reproducible way to estimate classification performance in ultra-low-replication screening workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a model-based framework that derives classification metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUROC) from the strictly standardized mean difference (SSMD) for high-throughput screening assays with ultra-low replication (e.g., single-replicate designs). Using closed-form relationships under a Gaussian equal-variance assumption, the framework provides explicit estimators and exact confidence intervals from the noncentral t-distribution, offering a more stable and meaningful alternative to classical statistical power for hit selection in sparse screening data.
AI.motivation: High-throughput screening (HTS) assays suffer from extreme data sparsity (typically single-replicate measurements), making conventional machine-learning metrics like sensitivity, specificity, and AUROC difficult to estimate reliably because they require adequately sized labeled samples.
AI.method: Derives closed-form relationships linking SSMD to Youden-optimal sensitivity/specificity and sensitivity at preset specificity under a Gaussian equal-variance assumption. Provides explicit estimators and exact confidence intervals from the noncentral t-distribution, applicable even under single-replicate designs.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a hepatitis C virus primary siRNA screen (~22,000 single-replicate measurements), showing that SSMD, AUROC, and sensitivity-based thresholds yield equivalent and interpretable hit sets. SSMD-derived sensitivity converges to a finite population value reflecting true group separation, unlike classical statistical power which approaches 1 with sample size.
AI.conclusion: This work bridges classical HTS statistics and machine-learning evaluation theory, providing a statistically principled and reproducible approach for estimating classification performance in ultra-low-replication screening workflows.

title: Nuclear mechanics controls the temporal dynamics of cell unjamming
summary: Cell unjamming in dense tissues is a complex but essential process in embryogenesis and cancer metastasis. Increasing evidence suggests that nuclear mechanics and density effects play a vital role in collective cell unjamming. However, state-of-the-art cell-shape-based theories fail to include nuclear and density effects, while computer models featuring rigid nuclei disagree with experimental observations of elongated nuclei promoting unjamming. Here, we introduce a computational model of confluent cells with explicitly deformable nuclei to study the dynamics of cell unjamming. Our simulations show an unjamming transition controlled by nuclear size and shape, reconciling conflicting theories of density-driven versus shape-driven mechanisms. We predict general relations connecting cellular and nuclear shape to collective cell motion, verified experimentally in distinct monolayers of MCF-10A and MDA-MB-436 breast cells, with striking accuracy. Our work establishes a rational connection between nuclear mechanics and tissue-scale rigidity transitions, highlighting the nucleus's key role in collective cell unjamming.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a computational model of confluent cells with explicitly deformable nuclei to study cell unjamming in dense tissues. The simulations reveal an unjamming transition controlled by nuclear size and shape, reconciling conflicting shape-driven versus density-driven theories, and are verified experimentally in breast cell monolayers with striking accuracy.
AI.motivation: Cell unjamming is crucial for embryogenesis and cancer metastasis, but existing cell-shape-based theories fail to account for nuclear mechanics and density effects. Computer models with rigid nuclei contradict experimental observations showing elongated nuclei promote unjamming.
AI.method: The authors develop a computational model of confluent cells with explicitly deformable nuclei to simulate the dynamics of cell unjamming, incorporating nuclear size and shape as key variables.
AI.result: Simulations show an unjamming transition controlled by nuclear size and shape, reconciling density-driven versus shape-driven mechanisms. The model predicts general relations between cellular/nuclear shape and collective cell motion, verified in MCF-10A and MDA-MB-436 breast cell monolayers with striking accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a rational connection between nuclear mechanics and tissue-scale rigidity transitions, highlighting the nucleus's key role in collective cell unjamming and providing a unified framework that bridges conflicting theories.

title: Low-frequency output fluctuations in an open exclusion process with particle pausing
summary: Slow internal states reshape both the mean throughput and the temporal organization of a driven lattice gas. Exit-counting statistics reveal this effect in a finite open totally asymmetric simple exclusion process whose particles reversibly switch between active and paused states. Increasing pausing lowers the mean current smoothly, whereas the long-window Fano factor is strongly nonmonotonic. At the reference boundary rates, the maximum remains near a measured mean paused population \(N_p=Lρ_{\rm paused}\simeq1.5\)--\(2\) across lattice lengths L=50-500, while the corresponding pausing rate scales as \(k_p^{\rm max}\propto L^{-1}\). A minimal constant-birth, linear-death approximation translates an order-one collective crossover into this finite-size displacement and gives \(N_p^\star\simeq1.50\) in the independent-pause, strong-blocking limit. The simulations delimit this approximation: the pause number is overdispersed, and at fixed \(N_p\), slower unpausing increases both the correlation time and the noise amplitude. Residence-time and structural analyses further separate the relevant slow variables. The pause-free versus pause-containing residence-time scale tracks the fitted output-correlation time, whereas the noise amplitude follows fluctuations, rather than the mean size, of the largest particle cluster. Low-frequency output noise therefore identifies an intermittent finite-size regime shaped jointly by slow-defect kinetics and traffic-jam reorganization.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a driven lattice gas (open TASEP) where particles reversibly switch between active and paused states. Pausing smoothly reduces mean current but strongly nonmonotonically affects long-window Fano factor, with maximum noise near mean paused population ~1.5-2 particles, and optimal pausing rate scaling as L^-1. A minimal approximation predicts N_p*≈1.50, and simulations show the pause number is overdispersed while slower unpausing increases correlation time and noise amplitude, linking low-frequency noise to interplay of slow-defect kinetics and traffic-jam reorganization.
AI.motivation: To understand how slow internal states (particle pausing) reshape both the mean throughput and temporal organization of a driven lattice gas, particularly via exit-counting statistics, revealing an intermittent finite-size regime.
AI.method: Finite open TASEP with particles switching between active and paused states; exit-counting statistics, Fano factor analysis, mean paused population measurements, minimal constant-birth/linear-death approximation, residence-time and structural (cluster-fluctuation) analyses, computer simulations across lattice lengths L=50-500.
AI.result: Increasing pausing lowers mean current smoothly; Fano factor is strongly nonmonotonic. Maximum noise occurs at N_p≈1.5-2 across L=50-500, with k_p^max∝L^-1. Approximation predicts N_p*≈1.50. Simulations show pause number is overdispersed; slower unpausing increases correlation time and noise amplitude. Noise amplitude follows fluctuations (not mean) of largest particle cluster.
AI.conclusion: Low-frequency output noise identifies an intermittent finite-size regime shaped jointly by slow-defect kinetics and traffic-jam reorganization, with the pause number being a robust critical quantity and cluster-size fluctuations controlling noise amplitude.

title: Predicting blood clot growth from sparse post-onset measurements with latent neural differential equations
summary: Computational models of blood clotting improve understanding of thrombus formation, but their clinical application remains limited because many model inputs are difficult to measure and patient-specific data are often sparse. We present a computational framework based on latent neural differential equations that infers unknown model parameters from sparse measurements and forecasts thrombosis progression. We demonstrate the framework using data generated from a multiphysics blood-clotting model in which clot growth is governed by the coagulation cascade and diffusion. Four known biochemical inputs (fibrinogen and factors IX, VIII, and V), together with sparse early clot-size observations, are used to infer the tissue-factor parameter and predict subsequent clot growth. We compare seven probabilistic methods: stochastic neural ordinary differential equations (SNODE), stochastic neural functional differential equations (SNFDE), a latent neural-process baseline, a monotone probabilistic deep ensemble, empirical trajectory retrieval, PCA-ridge Gaussian posterior, and Gompertz-curve retrieval. SNODE achieved the best performance in inferring the unknown input and forecasting future clot-growth trajectories. SNFDE performed similarly and consistently outperformed the other non-differential models. Prediction accuracy improved as more observations became available, whereas longer forecasting horizons increased uncertainty and decreased accuracy. Latent neural differential equations thus effectively combine parameter inference and clot-growth forecasting from sparse measurements, providing a promising foundation for personalized thrombosis modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational framework using latent neural differential equations to infer unknown blood-clotting parameters from sparse patient data and forecast thrombosis progression. SNODE and SNFDE outperformed five other probabilistic methods when tested on data from a multiphysics clotting model.
AI.motivation: Clinical application of blood-clotting computational models is limited because many model inputs are difficult to measure and patient-specific data are sparse.
AI.method: A framework based on latent neural differential equations (SNODE, SNFDE, etc.) that infers unknown tissue-factor parameters from four known biochemical inputs and sparse early clot-size observations, then forecasts subsequent clot growth. Seven probabilistic methods were compared.
AI.result: SNODE achieved the best performance in parameter inference and clot-growth forecasting. SNFDE performed similarly and outperformed non-differential models. Accuracy improved with more observations but declined with longer forecasting horizons.
AI.conclusion: Latent neural differential equations effectively combine parameter inference with clot-growth forecasting from sparse measurements, providing a promising foundation for personalized thrombosis modeling.

title: $\texttt{DisMorph}$: learning to disentangle technical distortions from true biological change
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, longitudinal morphometry, deformable registration, neuroimaging, domain randomization, gradient non-linearity distortion, accepted by the SASHIMI Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Longitudinal MRI enables sensitive measurement of structural brain change for studying aging and neurodegenerative disease. Deformable image registration is a key tool for estimating such change by computing a dense deformation that captures geometric differences between longitudinal scans. However, MRI scanners introduce geometric distortions that vary across acquisition systems and protocols, such as gradient non-linearity (GNL) distortion. Existing registration methods estimate a single field that conflates biological and technical effects, potentially biasing downstream morphometric measurements if distortions remain (partially) uncorrected. We propose $\texttt{DisMorph}$, a registration framework trained entirely on synthetic data that explicitly decomposes longitudinal deformation into technical and anatomical transforms. It predicts two dense deformations, each encoding one effect. During training, a novel generative model synthesizes both effects separately to provide disentanglement supervision, while domain randomization promotes generalization across imaging protocols. We evaluate our method in three complementary settings. On simulated data with known ground truth, our method detects anatomical change more accurately and consistently than conventional registration. On real image pairs that differ only by GNL distortion, our method assigns most geometric change to the distortion field, demonstrating specificity in the absence of anatomical change. On longitudinal Alzheimer's disease (AD) pairs, our method detects anatomical change in AD-related brain structures while identifying residual distortion left after standard correction. By disentangling MRI-induced distortion from biological change in the longitudinal deformation, our method paves the way for more accurate longitudinal morphometry in clinical settings where maintaining acquisition consistency is challenging.

AI.tldr: DisMorph is a registration framework trained on synthetic data that decomposes longitudinal MRI deformation into technical (gradient non-linearity distortion) and anatomical (biological change) components, improving accuracy of structural brain change measurement.
AI.motivation: MRI scanners introduce geometric distortions (e.g., gradient non-linearity) that vary across systems and protocols. Existing registration methods conflate biological and technical effects in a single deformation field, potentially biasing morphometric measurements in longitudinal studies.
AI.method: DisMorph is trained entirely on synthetic data that separately synthesizes technical and anatomical effects, providing disentanglement supervision. It predicts two dense deformations, one for each effect, using domain randomization for generalization across imaging protocols.
AI.result: On simulated data, DisMorph detects anatomical change more accurately/consistently than conventional registration. On real GNL-only image pairs, it correctly assigns geometric change to the distortion field. On longitudinal AD pairs, it detects anatomical change in AD-related structures while identifying residual distortion.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling MRI-induced distortion from biological change enables more accurate longitudinal morphometry, especially in clinical settings where maintaining acquisition consistency is challenging.

title: VOICE: A Vision-Omics Foundation Model Integrating Direct and Retrieval-Based Prediction of In-situ Single-Cell Gene Expression
summary: Spatial transcriptomics can resolve gene expression at single-cell resolution, but it is costly, limited to targeted panels of a few hundred to a few thousand genes, and applicable to only a small number of samples. H&E imaging, by contrast, is cheap and collected routinely at scale. This makes predicting single-cell expression directly from morphology a practical way to bring molecular analysis to large tissue archives. We therefore present VOICE, a multimodal foundation model that predicts single-cell gene expression from H&E images using paired Xenium data. VOICE first aligns cell centered H&E morphology from a pathology foundation model with single-cell expression embeddings from a transcriptome foundation model, trained using contrastive learning over 23 million cells. Next it predicts expression through two branches. One branch directly regresses expression from morphology. The other branch retrieves measured expression from similar reference cells, recovering genes that do not have morphological signal. Because genes vary in morphological predictability, VOICE fuses the two branches with a per-gene weight. After training, VOICE generalizes to heldout patients, slides, and partially overlapping gene panels from Xenium, and it consistently outperforms prior single-cell expression prediction methods on seven metrics.

AI.tldr: VOICE is a multimodal foundation model that predicts single-cell gene expression from H&E images using paired Xenium spatial transcriptomics data, trained via contrastive learning over 23 million cells, combining direct regression and reference-based retrieval branches with per-gene fusion weights.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly, limited to targeted gene panels, and applicable to few samples, while H&E imaging is cheap and routine. Predicting single-cell expression from morphology would enable molecular analysis at scale on large tissue archives.
AI.method: VOICE aligns cell-centered H&E morphology embeddings (from a pathology foundation model) with single-cell expression embeddings (from a transcriptome foundation model) via contrastive learning over 23M cells. It then uses two branches: one regresses expression directly from morphology, the other retrieves measured expression from similar reference cells. The two branches are fused with a per-gene weight to account for varying morphological predictability of genes.
AI.result: VOICE generalizes to held-out patients, slides, and partially overlapping Xenium gene panels, consistently outperforming prior single-cell expression prediction methods on seven metrics.
AI.conclusion: Predicting single-cell gene expression from routine H&E images is feasible at scale, bringing molecular analysis to large tissue archives via multimodal foundation modeling.

title: Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: generalising the work of Hill and Kac
summary: In a preceding paper, we used the graph-theoretic linear framework to show how transient properties of continuous-time Markov processes -- splitting probabilities and the moments of first-passage time (FPT) distributions -- could be expressed as rational algebraic functions of the transition rates, by using spanning forests of the underlying graph. This contrasts with the related rational formulas for steady-state (s.s.) probabilities, which use only spanning trees. The biophysicist Terrell Hill sketched a procedure for calculating mean FPTs and splitting probabilities in terms of the s.s. probabilities of a modified Markov process, thereby converting calculations using ensembles of trajectories to those using a single trajectory. Similarly, Mark Kac showed that the mean recurrence time to a state of a Markov process could be expressed in terms of the s.s. probability of that state. Here, we explore further the relationships between transient and s.s. properties, forests and trees, and ensemble and single-trajectory calculations. We formalise Hill's procedure by introducing a Hill operator, $H_u[G]$, on a graph, $G$, and use it to calculate all moments of the conditional and unconditional FPTs from $u$ as rational functions of the s.s. probabilities of $H_u[G]$, which arise from trees and "exchange factors" which arise from forests. We then combine this with an unravelling operator, $U_v[G]$, to calculate all moments of the recurrence time distribution as rational functions of the s.s. probabilities of $G$ and related exchange factors. Surprisingly, the Hill operator turns out to be a left-inverse to the unravelling operator, suggesting that the algebra of operators on linear framework graphs may be of broader interest. Our results integrate and generalise previously disparate findings into a common repertoire of rational algebraic formulas for FPTs of Markov processes.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes and generalizes connections between transient properties (first-passage times, splitting probabilities) and steady-state properties of continuous-time Markov processes using the graph-theoretic linear framework. The authors introduce a Hill operator and an unravelling operator on graphs, showing that all moments of first-passage-time distributions and recurrence time distributions can be expressed as rational functions of steady-state probabilities and exchange factors. Remarkably, the Hill operator is a left-inverse of the unravelling operator, unifying previously disparate results by Terrell Hill and Mark Kac into a common algebraic framework.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to deepen the theoretical connection between transient and steady-state properties of Markov processes. While prior work (by the same authors) showed transient properties can be expressed via spanning forests and steady-state properties via spanning trees, and while Hill and Kac had sketched individual results relating mean first-passage times to steady-state probabilities, a unified formal framework was missing. The authors seek to formalize these scattered findings and generalize them to all moments of FPT and recurrence time distributions.
AI.method: The authors work within the graph-theoretic linear framework for continuous-time Markov processes. They introduce two operators on graphs: (1) the Hill operator H_u[G], which formalizes Hill's procedure by modifying the graph so that transient properties (all moments of conditional and unconditional FPTs from state u) can be computed as rational functions of the steady-state probabilities of the modified graph—these require trees and "exchange factors" derived from forests; (2) the unravelling operator U_v[G], which combined with the Hill operator allows computation of all moments of the recurrence time distribution as rational functions of the steady-state probabilities of the original graph G plus related exchange factors. They then analyze the algebraic relationships between these operators.
AI.result: The paper derives rational algebraic formulas for all moments of conditional and unconditional FPT distributions and for all moments of recurrence time distributions, expressed in terms of steady-state probabilities and exchange factors. A key surprising finding is that the Hill operator is a left-inverse to the unravelling operator, revealing an algebraic structure among operators on linear framework graphs. The results integrate and generalize previously disparate findings from Hill, Kac, and the authors' own prior work into a unified framework.
AI.conclusion: The work successfully formalizes Hill's procedure via the Hill operator and connects it with the unravelling operator, revealing a rich algebraic structure. It demonstrates that transient and steady-state properties of Markov processes can be unified within a common graph-theoretic algebraic framework, converting ensemble-of-trajectory calculations into single-trajectory (steady-state) calculations. The discovery that H_u is a left-inverse of U_v suggests that the operator algebra on linear framework graphs may have broader mathematical and biophysical significance.

title: A General Theory for Phenotypic Association in Biological Systems
summary: Biological recognition rarely rests on one strong bond. It works by forming many weak ones at once, between crowded, deformable surfaces in water. This review develops that process as a problem in statistical mechanics. Counting the ways two multivalent objects can bind proves to be the classical monomer-dimer problem on a graph, with a rigorous consequence: the apparent switching of multivalent binding is always a smooth crossover, never a phase transition. Three constraints follow. A repulsive surface layer is obligatory rather than a design choice; bonds do not act independently; and since free energies enter rates exponentially, small changes in receptor number shift binding lifetimes by orders of magnitude. One set of equations then covers antibodies, lipoproteins, and T cell recognition. In each, what decides the outcome is not the strength of any single bond but how a fixed total is spread over many: affinity is a property of a molecule, selectivity a property of an assembly.

AI.tldr: This review frames multivalent biological recognition as a statistical mechanics problem, showing that multivalent binding is the classical monomer-dimer problem on a graph, with the key result that apparent switching in multivalent binding is always a smooth crossover rather than a phase transition. Three constraints follow: repulsive surface layers are obligatory, bonds are not independent, and small receptor number changes exponentially shift binding lifetimes. A single set of equations covers antibodies, lipoproteins, and T cell recognition, where affinity is a property of a single molecule but selectivity emerges from the assembly.
AI.motivation: To understand how biological recognition works through many weak simultaneous bonds between crowded, deformable surfaces in water, and to develop a unified statistical mechanics framework that explains multivalent binding across diverse biological systems.
AI.method: The review reformulates multivalent binding as a problem in statistical mechanics, mapping it to the classical monomer-dimer problem on a graph. From this mathematical equivalence, rigorous consequences and constraints are derived, which are then applied to a unified set of equations describing antibodies, lipoproteins, and T cell recognition.
AI.result: The analysis proves that multivalent binding apparent switching is always a smooth crossover, never a phase transition. It identifies three constraints: obligatory repulsive surface layers, non-independent bond behavior, and exponential sensitivity of binding lifetimes to receptor number. The framework successfully describes multiple biological systems with a single mathematical structure.
AI.conclusion: The outcome of biological recognition is determined not by the strength of any single bond, but by how a fixed total is distributed over many bonds. Affinity is a property of an individual molecule, while selectivity is a property of the assembly as a whole.

title: Physical limits to concentration and gradient sensing by perfect monitors
summary: Cells often estimate chemical concentrations from only a few diffusing molecules, whose stochastic motion limits sensing precision. We consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records the instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly. Here we derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing. Variance minimization maps to an electrostatic problem. Surprisingly, although the instrument monitors the entire volume, the optimal estimator assigns all weight to its boundary, reducing the uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing. We extend the results to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the optimal spatial weighting for concentration and gradient sensing from limited diffusing molecules. The variance minimization problem maps to electrostatics, revealing that the optimal estimator assigns all weight to the boundary of the monitored region, improving precision over the uniform Berg-Purcell estimator.
AI.motivation: Cells estimate chemical concentrations from only a few diffusing molecules, where stochastic motion limits sensing precision. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly, but it is unclear whether this is optimal. The authors aim to find the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing.
AI.method: The authors consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. They derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators by mapping the variance minimization problem to an electrostatic problem.
AI.result: The optimal estimator assigns all weight to the boundary of the monitored volume, reducing uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing compared to the uniform weighting. Results extend to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Despite monitoring the entire volume, the optimal sensing strategy focuses entirely on boundary measurements, providing a counterintuitive improvement in sensing precision over uniform volumetric weighting.

title: Idea Search: Guiding Tree Search with Ideas to Explore Diverse Scientific Methods
summary: Tree Search-based test-time scaling of LLMs is a powerful tool for automated scientific coding. However, pure Tree Search sometimes struggles with systematic exploration, becoming trapped in local optima, or unproductive loops, especially in the vast search space of scientific methods. To address this limitation, we propose Idea Search, a framework that systematically integrates a dynamic "Idea Bank" into Tree Search. Idea Search involves three steps: (1) decomposing existing methods into atomic ideas, (2) sampling from this bank of ideas to guide branches of code mutations, and (3) dynamically updating the bank with new ideas discovered through execution. On single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) batch integration, Idea Search reliably breaks the plateau of a strong pure Tree Search baseline, improving the mean score from 0.678 to 0.697 and reaching a best score of 0.728. We then characterize which design choices drive these gains: bank augmentation helps bandit sampling but not random sampling, "Exploratory" prompting that prioritizes new ideas surfaces the rare best-performing solutions, while increasing sampling-level exploration is counterproductive.

AI.tldr: Idea Search is a framework that integrates a dynamic "Idea Bank" into Tree Search for test-time scaling of LLMs in scientific coding, improving performance on scRNA-seq batch integration from 0.678 to 0.697 mean score (0.728 best) by decomposing methods into atomic ideas, sampling from them to guide code mutations, and dynamically updating the bank.
AI.motivation: Pure Tree Search struggles with systematic exploration in the vast search space of scientific methods, often getting trapped in local optima or unproductive loops, limiting its effectiveness for automated scientific coding tasks.
AI.method: Idea Search has three steps: (1) decomposing existing methods into atomic ideas, (2) sampling from a dynamic "Idea Bank" to guide branches of code mutations, and (3) updating the bank with new ideas discovered through execution feedback.
AI.result: On scRNA-seq batch integration, Idea Search improves mean score from 0.678 to 0.697 and reaches a best score of 0.728. Design choices analysis shows bank augmentation helps bandit sampling but not random sampling, "Exploratory" prompting surfaces rare best-performing solutions, and increasing sampling-level exploration is counterproductive.
AI.conclusion: Systematically integrating a dynamic Idea Bank into Tree Search reliably breaks plateaus of pure Tree Search baselines, demonstrating the importance of structured idea reuse and selective exploration for test-time scaling in scientific coding.

title: Reading Cognition as Decisions Unfold in Words: A Factorized Inverse Decision Model
summary: Inverse decision modeling infers latent properties of decision processes from observed behavior, but existing formulations rely primarily on action trajectories. In verbalized cognitive tasks, task execution also produces response dynamics that action-only formulations leave unmodeled, such as verbal production, interaction, and hesitation. We propose a factorized inverse decision model (FIDM) that decomposes each individual's task-execution likelihood into an action factor and an effort factor, governed by separate individual-specific parameters. From raw verbal transcripts, a language model produces structured task-execution traces for factorized inference. On data from 400 older adults performing a grocery-shopping dialog task for cognitive screening, controlled recovery shows selective estimation of the intended factors, while matched semi-synthetic conditions show that FIDM preserves action-execution distinctions even when aggregate behavioral summaries are matched. Action evidence further localizes task-defined deviations across participants. In cognitive-status classification, FIDM provides information complementary to clinical scores, trajectory summaries, and frozen language representations, with consistent gains across all evaluated baselines in the binary setting.

AI.tldr: FIDM decomposes task-execution likelihood into action and effort factors for verbalized cognitive tasks, improving inverse decision modeling by modeling response dynamics beyond action trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing inverse decision models focus on action trajectories and ignore response dynamics in verbalized cognitive tasks (verbal production, interaction, hesitation).
AI.method: Factorized inverse decision model (FIDM) with separate individual-specific parameters for action and effort factors; language model extracts structured traces from raw transcripts for factorized inference.
AI.result: On 400 older adults in a grocery-shopping dialog task: controlled recovery shows selective factor estimation; FIDM preserves action distinctions even with matched semi-synthetic conditions; action evidence localizes task deviations; FIDM yields consistent gains across all baselines in binary cognitive-status classification.
AI.conclusion: FIDM provides complementary information to clinical scores and language representations, demonstrating the value of modeling effort-related response dynamics in inverse decision modeling for cognitive assessment.

title: Flow-based conditional cardiac anatomy generation for virtual cohorts
summary: Cardiac digital twin research is moving from subject-specific anatomical replicas toward virtual cohorts that represent clinically relevant population subgroups. Yet access to representative imaging-derived anatomy datasets remains limited by cohort size, subgroup sparsity, and data-sharing constraints. Conditional generative models could help address this gap, but virtual cohorts are useful only if they preserve realistic, metadata-dependent anatomical variability. Existing cardiac anatomy generators largely rely on conditional variational autoencoders (cVAEs), which couple representation learning and metadata conditioning through a shared regularized latent prior. We introduce CAN-FLOW, a two-step Conditional ANatomy generation framework based on normalizing FLOWs that first learns geometry-only latent representations of diffeomorphic cardiac shape momenta and then models their sex-, age-, and body-mass-index-dependent distribution with a conditional normalizing flow. We trained CAN-FLOW on 2,208 healthy UK Biobank subjects and compared it with cVAEs across regularization strengths. CAN-FLOW generated plausible stochastic biventricular anatomies that better reproduced clinical phenotype distributions, metadata-dependent trends, subgroup variability, point-cloud coverage, and high-dimensional shape variability. Together, these results establish CAN-FLOW as a shareable framework for generating realistic, stochastically varying, metadata-conditioned biventricular anatomies for virtual cohort construction and in silico clinical trial workflows.

AI.tldr: CAN-FLOW is a two-step conditional anatomy generation framework using normalizing flows to generate realistic, metadata-conditioned (sex, age, BMI) biventricular cardiac anatomies for virtual cohort construction, outperforming cVAE baselines on 2,208 UK Biobank subjects.
AI.motivation: Cardiac digital twin research needs virtual cohorts representing clinically relevant population subgroups, but imaging-derived anatomical datasets are limited by cohort size, subgroup sparsity, and data-sharing constraints. Existing generative models (cVAEs) couple representation learning with metadata conditioning through shared regularized latent priors, which limits their ability to preserve realistic metadata-dependent anatomical variability.
AI.method: CAN-FLOW is a two-step Conditional ANatomy generation framework: (1) it first learns geometry-only latent representations of diffeomorphic cardiac shape momenta, then (2) models their sex-, age-, and BMI-dependent distribution using a conditional normalizing flow. This decouples representation learning from metadata conditioning, unlike cVAEs which couple them via a shared regularized latent prior.
AI.result: Trained on 2,208 healthy UK Biobank subjects, CAN-FLOW generated plausible stochastic biventricular anatomies that better reproduced clinical phenotype distributions, metadata-dependent trends, subgroup variability, point-cloud coverage, and high-dimensional shape variability compared to cVAEs across various regularization strengths.
AI.conclusion: CAN-FLOW establishes a shareable framework for generating realistic, stochastically varying, metadata-conditioned biventricular anatomies, advancing virtual cohort construction and in silico clinical trial workflows in cardiac digital twin research.
